frase_gancho.texto: A clay goddess, almost life-size, who died in childbirth.

puente_narrativo.texto: A woman who accompanies the Sun. Now look for a young man made of stone, slender and naked, with half his body carved with maize plants and a child on his back.

guion_corto.texto: This fired clay figure measures one meter forty-eight centimeters: almost the size of a person. It comes from El Zapotal, in Veracruz, and is identified as a Cihuateteo, a “divine woman”: this was what they called women who died in childbirth. She sits with her hands on her knees, her torso bare and a necklace of beads. A long skirt is held by a belt from which serpents peek out. Her face has fixed eyes and a slightly open mouth, and on her head she wears a large headdress with the figure of a reptile. For the peoples of Mesoamerica, these women were warriors: dying in childbirth was equivalent to dying in combat, and it was believed that from then on they accompanied the Sun.

guion_largo.texto:
Look at those eyes. They are fixed on something you cannot see. This seated, serene woman of clay is no ordinary person: she is the memory of a woman who died at the most dangerous moment of life, and who for that reason became a goddess.

To understand the idea, go back for a moment to the Mexica Hall, where you saw [Tlaltecuhtli in a squatting position](mna_s06_tlaltecuhtli), in the posture of childbirth. In the Mexica world, giving birth was a battle. The sources say that the midwife encouraged the woman as one would a warrior in battle: each child was a captured prisoner. If the mother died, she did not go to Mictlán, the place of the common dead. She had the destiny of a fallen warrior.

You already saw it with the [Eagle Warrior](mna_s06_guerrero_aguila): soldiers who died in combat accompanied the Sun from dawn until midday. The women who died in childbirth then received it, and accompanied it from midday until sunset, toward the west, which was called Cihuatlampa, “the direction of the women.” The men raised it into the sky; the women lowered it.

But these goddesses were also frightening. It was believed that on certain days they descended to earth by the crossroads, and that they could make children ill. The sources tell that some soldiers tried to steal a finger or a lock of hair from one of these dead women, because they believed it gave courage in combat. For that reason, these same sources say, the family guarded the body for several nights. A goddess admired, revered and also feared. According to the Mexica sources, offerings of food were left for them at crossroads, to appease them.

There are even those who connect these women with a legend you surely know. Among the omens said to have occurred in the last years before the conquest, there was one of a woman who wept at night through the streets, and who cried out for her children. Some authors have seen in her an ancestor of the Llorona. There is no way to prove it, but it shows how certain figures from antiquity remain alive in the popular imagination.

This figure was found at El Zapotal, in central Veracruz, in a funerary sanctuary dedicated to the god of death, where several life-size clay figures surrounded an altar. There is an important detail: this clay is earlier, by centuries, than the Mexica empire. That tells us that the idea of the woman who died in childbirth as a divine warrior was not born in Tenochtitlan: it is much older and was widespread across several regions.

Notice how it was made. A hollow figure of this size is difficult to fire without breaking. It is thought that it was modeled in sections, which were then joined, and that the whole piece went through the fire. Traces of paint remain on its surface, so it was not the color of clay: it was painted. And the belt of serpents, the headdress with a reptile and the fixed eyes give her an air of trance, of a gaze that pierces time.

This is a piece that changes how we imagine women in ancient religion. They were not a secondary role: they had their own path in the sky, their own direction of the world and their own battle.

texto: Look at her eyes and her slightly open mouth: what expression does she have?
Find the serpent heads on the belt
Observe the headdress: what animal appears on it?

texto.pregunta: Myth: Women had a secondary role in the religion of Mesoamerica.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Those who died in childbirth were revered as divine warriors and were believed to accompany the Sun on its path across the sky.
